CALIFORNIA STATE TRADEMARK REGISTRATION (MODEL STATE TRADEMARK LAW) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Acme, Inc. · 500 Market St, San Francisco, CA 94105

CALIFORNIA STATE TRADEMARK REGISTRATION INFORMATION SHEET — PURPOSE AND SCOPE
This information sheet relates to Acme, Inc., having a business address at 500 Market St, San Francisco, CA 94105, concerning the mark described as The word mark "ACME" in standard characters, used on or in connection with Retail sale of outdoor recreational equipment, claimed to have first been used anywhere on March 3, 2024 and first used in California on June 15, 2024. It describes California's own state-level trademark and service mark registration system — the Model State Trademark Law, codified at California Business and Professions Code Sections 14200 through 14272 and administered by the California Secretary of State — including who may apply, what an application must contain, the grounds on which the Secretary of State may refuse registration, the examination and priority procedure, what a certificate of registration shows and proves, the five-year renewable term, the grounds on which a registration may be canceled, and how this state registration system relates to a federal trademark registration and to common-law trademark rights. This document is not this project's Trademark Registration (USPTO Application) Information Sheet, Trademark Assignment Agreement Information Sheet, or Fictitious Business Name (DBA) Statement document. Those documents concern, respectively: registration of a mark with the United States Patent and Trademark Office under the federal Lanham Act; the assignment of an already-registered mark (state or federal); and a county-level filing that discloses the true owner of a business operating under a name other than its legal name, which identifies a business, not a source of goods or services. A California state trademark or service mark registration is a further and separate filing, made with the California Secretary of State rather than a county recorder or the USPTO, and it protects a word, name, symbol, or device used to identify and distinguish goods or services — not a business's legal or fictitious name as such, though the same wording can sometimes serve both functions. A business can hold a fictitious business name statement, a federal trademark registration, both, or neither, and can separately hold, or not hold, a California state trademark or service mark registration; none of these filings substitutes for any other. This information sheet is informational only. It does not itself register any mark for Acme, Inc. or any other person, does not determine whether The word mark "ACME" in standard characters qualifies for registration under California or federal law, and does not constitute legal advice.

THE MODEL STATE TRADEMARK LAW AND WHAT COUNTS AS A REGISTRABLE MARK
California's state-level trademark statute is formally named by its own text: the chapter of the Business and Professions Code governing state registration "shall be known and may be cited as the Model State Trademark Law." That chapter defines a "trademark," for purposes of state registration, as any word, name, symbol, or device, or any combination of those, used by a person to identify and distinguish that person's goods from goods manufactured or sold by others and to indicate the source of the goods, even where that source is not otherwise known to the public. A parallel, separately worded definition in the same section covers a "service mark" on the same terms but for services rather than goods, and further provides that titles, character names, and other distinctive features of radio or television programs may themselves be registered as service marks even though they, or the programs carrying them, may advertise a sponsor's goods. The statute's own defined term "mark" is broader still: it includes any trademark or service mark entitled to registration under this chapter, whether or not it has actually been registered.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "This chapter shall be known and may be cited as the Model State Trademark Law."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 14200, Model State Trademark Law, short title (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=14200.)
  "“Trademark” means any word, name, symbol, or device, or any combination thereof, used by a person to identify and distinguish the goods of that person, including a unique product, from those manufactured or sold by others, and to indicate the source of the goods, even if that source is unknown."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 14202(a), California's statutory definition of "trademark" for state registration (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=14202.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only two of California Business and Professions Code Section 14202's fifteen lettered definitions — subdivision (a) ("trademark") and, by paraphrase rather than direct quotation, subdivision (b) ("service mark") — and Section 14200's short-title sentence; both cited sections are subdivisions of, or the whole of, two independently enacted sections of the same chapter, not a single unified definitions list restated here in full. Section 14202 separately defines "mark," "trade name," "person," "applicant," "registrant," "use," "abandoned," "secretary," "dilution," "dilution by blurring," "dilution by tarnishment," "counterfeit," and "comparative commercial advertising," none of which is quoted in this clause even where a later clause in this document uses the term (for example, "abandoned" appears in the refusal-grounds and cancellation clauses below without restating this section's own definition of it). This clause does not determine whether the specific mark described in this document in fact functions as a "trademark" or "service mark" as statutorily defined, which depends on facts about actual use that this document does not resolve.

REGISTRATION REQUIRES AN UNDERLYING "USE" OF THE MARK, STATUTORILY DEFINED
State registration under the Model State Trademark Law is built on an underlying, statutorily defined concept of "use." The statute defines "use" to mean the bona fide use of a mark in the ordinary course of trade, and specifically excludes a use made merely to reserve a right in a mark. The same section goes on to specify, in two further subdivisions, what counts as "in use" for goods (placement on the goods, their containers, displays, or tags, or on associated documents where physical placement is impracticable, coupled with the goods being sold or transported in commerce in California) and for services (use or display in the sale or advertising of services that are themselves rendered in California). That in-state-rendering and in-state-commerce framing is why an application under this chapter calls for two separate dates — the date of first use anywhere and the date of first use specifically in California — addressed in the application-contents clause below.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "“Use” means the bona fide use of a mark in the ordinary course of trade, and not made merely to reserve a right in a mark."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 14202(h), California's statutory definition of "use" for purposes of state trademark registration (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=14202.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only the lead sentence of Section 14202(h)'s "use" definition; the same subdivision's two further, numbered sub-parts describing in-state use for goods versus services are paraphrased here, not quoted verbatim, and a reader relying on this clause for the precise statutory wording of either sub-part should consult the section directly. This clause does not determine whether any specific, described use of the mark on or in connection with the goods or services identified in this document meets this statutory definition, which is a fact-specific determination this document does not make. Separately, Section 14202(i) defines "abandoned" to include, among other things, nonuse for two consecutive years as prima facie evidence of abandonment; that definition bears directly on the durability of any use-based rights described in this clause but is not quoted here.

STATUTORY GROUNDS ON WHICH THE SECRETARY OF STATE MAY REFUSE TO REGISTER A MARK
The Model State Trademark Law lists six independent criteria, any one of which bars registration of an otherwise-distinguishing mark. As enacted, the list includes marks that consist of or comprise immoral, deceptive, or scandalous matter; marks that disparage or falsely suggest a connection with a person, institution, belief, or national symbol, or that bring any of those into contempt or disrepute; flags, coats of arms, or other governmental insignia; a living individual's name, signature, or portrait used without that individual's written consent; marks that are merely descriptive, deceptively misdescriptive, primarily geographically descriptive or misdescriptive, or primarily merely a surname (each subject to a statutory exception where the mark has become distinctive of the applicant's goods or services through five years of continuous use in California); and, as the statute's own words provide, a mark that "consists of or comprises a mark that so resembles a mark registered in this state or a mark or trade name previously used by another and not abandoned, as to be likely, when used on or in connection with the goods or services of the applicant, to cause confusion or mistake, or to deceive."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "It consists of or comprises a mark that so resembles a mark registered in this state or a mark or trade name previously used by another and not abandoned, as to be likely, when used on or in connection with the goods or services of the applicant, to cause confusion or mistake, or to deceive."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 14205(f), grounds for refusing registration of a mark — likelihood of confusion with a previously registered or used mark or trade name (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=14205.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes verbatim only the sixth of Section 14205's six lettered refusal criteria, subdivision (f) (the likelihood-of-confusion ground); the other five are paraphrased, not quoted. More significantly, the first two criteria as written — barring marks that consist of or comprise "immoral, deceptive, or scandalous matter" (subdivision (a)) or matter that may "disparage" persons, institutions, or beliefs (subdivision (b)) — track language nearly identical to federal Lanham Act provisions that the United States Supreme Court held unconstitutional as viewpoint-based restrictions on speech in Matal v. Tam (2017) (the disparagement bar) and Iancu v. Brunetti (2019) (the "immoral or scandalous" bar). This document did not verify either of those decisions, or any California case addressing this state statute's own disparaging/immoral/scandalous language, against a primary source this session: CourtListener's search tool returned a rate-limit error ("429—Rate limit exceeded: 125/day") when queried for this topic, and no case-law citation is included anywhere in this document as a result. This clause should therefore not be read as confirming that Section 14205(a) or (b), as written on the books, is currently enforced by the Secretary of State as written; it reports only the statutory text found at leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, not any judicial narrowing or invalidation of it.

WHAT A STATE TRADEMARK APPLICATION MUST SET FORTH, INCLUDING TWO SEPARATE USE DATES
A person who uses a mark may file an application for its registration with the Secretary of State, on a form the Secretary prescribes, setting forth specified information, including the applicant's name and business address, the goods or services and the manner in which the mark is used on or in connection with them, a statement of the applicant's ownership and belief that no other person has a superior right to use the mark, and, as the statute specifically requires, "the date on which the mark was first used anywhere and the date when it was first used in this state by the applicant or a predecessor in interest." The application must include a declaration of accuracy, and the statute attaches a specific consequence to a knowingly false declaration: a person who "willfully states as true in the declaration a material fact that he or she knows to be false" is subject to a civil penalty of up to $10,000, enforceable in an action brought by a public prosecutor, and the statute requires that the declarant be informed of this penalty in writing. The Secretary may also require a statement of any related United States Patent and Trademark Office filing, a drawing of the mark, three specimens showing the mark as actually used, the application fee, and, if the mark is in a language other than English, a certified English translation.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The date on which the mark was first used anywhere and the date when it was first used in this state by the applicant or a predecessor in interest."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 14207(a)(3), required content of a state trademark application — date of first use anywhere and date of first use in California (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=14207.)
  "If the person signing the declaration willfully states as true in the declaration a material fact that he or she knows to be false, he or she shall be subject to a civil penalty of not more than ten thousand dollars ($10,000)."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 14207(d), civil penalty for a willfully false declaration of accuracy in a state trademark application (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=14207.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes two of Section 14207's several requirements — the dual first-use dates in subdivision (a)(3) and the false-declaration penalty in subdivision (d) — and paraphrases the rest; both citations are subdivisions of the same enacted section, not independent statutory sources. This clause does not itself state whether the first-use-anywhere and first-use-in-California dates given in this document would in fact satisfy the statute's dual-date requirement, and does not confirm whether the Secretary of State, as a matter of current administrative practice, still requires every item this 2008-enacted text describes (for example, the specimen and drawing requirements) exactly as written, since this document verified only the statutory text itself, not any current Secretary of State regulation, form instructions, or filing-fee schedule, none of which this document reproduces.

EXAMINATION, PRIORITY BETWEEN CONCURRENT APPLICATIONS, AND THE MANDAMUS REMEDY FOR A REFUSAL
After an application is filed and the fee paid, the Secretary of State may cause the application to be examined for conformity with the Model State Trademark Law, may request additional information or amendments, and, if the applicant is found not entitled to registration, must advise the applicant of the reasons and allow a specified period to reply or amend; this reply-and-reexamine cycle may repeat until the Secretary finally refuses registration or the applicant fails to respond, at which point the application is deemed abandoned. Where the Secretary is concurrently processing more than one application for the same or a confusingly similar mark covering the same or related goods or services, the statute resolves the conflict by filing date: "the secretary shall grant priority to the applications in the order of filing," with any rejected applicant then left to bring a statutory cancellation action against the prior-filed registrant. If the Secretary finally refuses registration, the statute gives the applicant a specific judicial remedy rather than an administrative appeal within the Secretary's own office: "the applicant may seek a writ of mandamus to compel registration," which "may be granted, but without costs to the secretary, on proof that all statements in the application are true and that the mark is otherwise entitled to registration."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "In the instance of applications concurrently being processed by the secretary seeking registration of the same or confusingly similar marks for the same or related goods or services, the secretary shall grant priority to the applications in the order of filing."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 14209(g), priority between concurrently processed applications for the same or confusingly similar mark (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=14209.)
  "If the secretary finally refuses registration of the mark, the applicant may seek a writ of mandamus to compel registration. A writ may be granted, but without costs to the secretary, on proof that all statements in the application are true and that the mark is otherwise entitled to registration."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 14209(f), writ of mandamus as the applicant's remedy for a final refusal of registration (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=14209.)
  Known gap: This clause's two citations are drawn from two subdivisions of the same enacted section, Section 14209(f) and (g), not independent statutory sources. The mandamus remedy described here runs against the Secretary of State's refusal to register; this clause does not describe, and this document does not separately address, any private right of action a competing mark owner might have to challenge a registration once issued, which is instead addressed by the cancellation clause below. This clause also does not state the ordinary time limit, if any, within which a mandamus petition must be filed following a final refusal, which this document did not locate in the text of this chapter.

THE CERTIFICATE OF REGISTRATION: WHAT IT STATES AND WHAT IT PROVES IN A CALIFORNIA COURT
Once an applicant has complied with the chapter's requirements, the statute directs that "the secretary shall cause a certificate of registration to be issued and delivered to the applicant," under the Secretary's signature and the seal of the state, showing the registrant's name and business address, the claimed dates of first use anywhere and first use in California, the class and description of the goods or services, a reproduction of the mark, and the registration date and term. The statute then gives that certificate a specific evidentiary role in state court: "any certificate of registration issued by the secretary under the provisions of this chapter or a copy thereof duly certified by the secretary shall be admissible in evidence as competent and sufficient proof of the registration of the mark in any action or judicial proceeding in any court of this state."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "Upon compliance by the applicant with the requirements of this chapter, the secretary shall cause a certificate of registration to be issued and delivered to the applicant."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 14215(a), issuance and required contents of a certificate of registration (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=14215.)
  "Any certificate of registration issued by the secretary under the provisions of this chapter or a copy thereof duly certified by the secretary shall be admissible in evidence as competent and sufficient proof of the registration of the mark in any action or judicial proceeding in any court of this state."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 14215(b), evidentiary effect of a certificate of registration in a California court (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=14215.)
  Known gap: This clause's two citations are drawn from two subdivisions of the same enacted section, Section 14215(a) and (b), not independent statutory sources. The statutory text quoted here makes the certificate proof of the fact of registration itself; it does not, on its own quoted terms, state that the certificate is prima facie evidence of the mark's validity, of the registrant's ownership, or of an exclusive right to use the mark in commerce — evidentiary presumptions that a different statute, the federal Lanham Act, expressly attaches to a federal registration certificate under 15 U.S.C. Section 1057(b), which this project's Trademark Registration (USPTO Application) Information Sheet document addresses and which this state-law clause does not restate or extend to state registration.

FIVE-YEAR RENEWABLE TERM
A state registration is time-limited and must be affirmatively renewed to continue. The statute provides that "a registration of mark pursuant to this chapter shall be effective for a term of five years from the date of registration and, upon application filed within six months prior to the expiration of the term, in a manner complying with the requirements of the secretary, the registration may be renewed for a like term from the end of the expiring term," accompanied by a renewal fee. The statute further provides that "a registration may be renewed for successive periods of five years in like manner," so that a registration can in principle be kept in force indefinitely through repeated five-year renewals. Every renewal application, whether of a registration made under this chapter or one carried over from a prior state trademark act, must include a verified statement that the mark has been and is still in use, together with a specimen showing that actual use.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "A registration of mark pursuant to this chapter shall be effective for a term of five years from the date of registration and, upon application filed within six months prior to the expiration of the term, in a manner complying with the requirements of the secretary, the registration may be renewed for a like term from the end of the expiring term."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 14217(a), five-year term of a state trademark registration and the renewal-filing window (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=14217.)
  "A registration may be renewed for successive periods of five years in like manner."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 14217(b), successive five-year renewal periods (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=14217.)
  Known gap: This clause's two citations are drawn from two subdivisions of the same enacted section, Section 14217(a) and (b), not independent statutory sources. The quoted text states a six-month pre-expiration renewal-filing window; this document did not locate, within this chapter's text, any express grace period or reinstatement procedure for a registration that lapses because no renewal application was filed within that window, and this clause does not state what becomes of an unrenewed registration beyond the fact that Section 14230, addressed in a separate clause below, lists a registration "not renewed in accordance with the provisions of this chapter" as one ground for cancellation.

GROUNDS ON WHICH THE SECRETARY OF STATE MUST CANCEL A REGISTRATION
The statute lists several distinct grounds requiring the Secretary of State to cancel a registration, in whole or in part: a voluntary request from the registrant or record assignee; a court finding that the registered mark has been abandoned, that the registrant is not the mark's owner, that the registration was granted improperly or obtained fraudulently, or that the mark has become the generic name for the goods or services it covers; a court-ordered cancellation on any ground; a dishonored payment check, following notice and a further 30-day cure period; and a registration issued in error within the preceding six months in violation of the confusing-similarity refusal ground. A separate, non-discretionary ground applies simply where a registration was "not renewed in accordance with the provisions of this chapter." The statute also addresses the specific interaction between a state registration and a prior federal one covering the same mark: where a state registration is challenged as confusingly similar to a mark registered earlier with the United States Patent and Trademark Office, "should the registrant prove that the registrant is the owner of a concurrent registration of a mark in the United States Patent and Trademark Office covering an area including this state, the registration hereunder shall not be canceled for that area of the state."

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "All registrations granted under this chapter and not renewed in accordance with the provisions of this chapter."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 14230(b), cancellation of a registration not renewed under this chapter (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=14230.)
  "However, should the registrant prove that the registrant is the owner of a concurrent registration of a mark in the United States Patent and Trademark Office covering an area including this state, the registration hereunder shall not be canceled for that area of the state."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 14230(c)(6), proviso protecting a registrant's concurrent federal registration from cancellation within its covered area (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=14230.)
  Known gap: This clause's two citations are drawn from two subdivisions of the same enacted section, Section 14230(b) and the proviso within subdivision (c)(6), not independent statutory sources; several of the other listed cancellation grounds are paraphrased rather than quoted. The federal-registration proviso quoted here protects a registrant only for "that area of the state" covered by the registrant's own concurrent federal registration — it does not, on its quoted terms, immunize the state registration statewide, and this clause does not attempt to state how "area" is determined or proven in a cancellation proceeding, which this document did not locate addressed elsewhere in this chapter's text.

STATE REGISTRATION'S OWN STATEMENT OF ITS RELATIONSHIP TO THE FEDERAL TRADEMARK SYSTEM
The Model State Trademark Law states its own intended relationship to the federal trademark system. The statute recites a legislative intent "to provide a system of state trademark registration and protection substantially consistent with the federal system of trademark registration and protection under the Trademark Act of 1946 (15 U.S.C. Sec. 1051 et seq.), as amended," and directs that federal case law construing the Lanham Act "should be examined as nonbinding authority for interpreting and construing this chapter" — meaning federal decisions inform, but do not control, how a California court or the Secretary of State applies this state statute. A California state registration remains, on this statute's own terms, a separate legal act from any federal registration or application with the United States Patent and Trademark Office; obtaining one does not itself obtain, or substitute for, the other. Separately from this state's relationship to the federal system, this chapter also expressly preserves common-law trademark rights that arise from actual use without any registration at all, a point addressed, with its own citation to this chapter, by this project's existing Trademark Infringement — Cease and Desist Letter Information Sheet document and not repeated here.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-06]
  "The intent of this chapter is to provide a system of state trademark registration and protection substantially consistent with the federal system of trademark registration and protection under the Trademark Act of 1946 (15 U.S.C. Sec. 1051 et seq.), as amended."
  — Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 14272, legislative intent that this chapter be substantially consistent with, and interpreted with reference to, the federal Lanham Act (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=BPC&sectionNum=14272.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only the first sentence of Section 14272; the statute's directive to examine federal case law as "nonbinding authority" runs in one direction — it tells a court how to interpret this state statute by reference to federal case law — and does not itself mean that a state registration confers any federal right, or that a federal registration confers any right under this state chapter. This clause does not identify, and this document does not cite, any actual California case applying Section 14272's interpretive cross-reference, because CourtListener's case-law search returned a rate-limit error ("429—Rate limit exceeded: 125/day") when queried this session, and no case law is cited anywhere in this document as a result. This clause also does not restate or re-cite Section 14259's separate preservation of common-law trademark rights, since that specific point, quoting that same section, already appears verbatim in this project's existing Trademark Infringement — Cease and Desist Letter Information Sheet document (clause id trademarkcd_ca_common_law_rights); a reader is directed there rather than to a duplicate restatement here.

The statute defines "use" to mean the bona fide use of a mark in the ordinary course of trade, and specifically excludes a use made merely to reserve a right in a mark. The same section goes on to specify, in two further subdivisions, what counts as "in use" for goods (placement on the goods, their containers, displays, or tags, or on associated documents where physical placement is impracticable, coupled with the goods being sold or transported in commerce in California) and for services (use or display in the sale or advertising of services that are themselves rendered in California). That in-state-rendering and in-state-commerce framing is why an application under this chapter calls for two separate dates — the date of first use anywhere and the date of first use specifically in California — addressed in the application-contents clause below.

citations.cite: California's statutory definition of "use" for purposes of state trademark registration
citations.quote: “Use” means the bona fide use of a mark in the ordinary course of trade, and not made merely to reserve a right in a mark.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause quotes only the lead sentence of Section 14202(h)'s "use" definition; the same subdivision's two further, numbered sub-parts describing in-state use for goods versus services are paraphrased here, not quoted verbatim, and a reader relying on this clause for the precise statutory wording of either sub-part should consult the section directly. This clause does not determine whether any specific, described use of the mark on or in connection with the goods or services identified in this document meets this statutory definition, which is a fact-specific determination this document does not make. Separately, Section 14202(i) defines "abandoned" to include, among other things, nonuse for two consecutive years as prima facie evidence of abandonment; that definition bears directly on the durability of any use-based rights described in this clause but is not quoted here.

expectedJSON.body: The Model State Trademark Law lists six independent criteria, any one of which bars registration of an otherwise-distinguishing mark. As enacted, the list includes marks that consist of or comprise immoral, deceptive, or scandalous matter; marks that disparage or falsely suggest a connection with a person, institution, belief, or national symbol, or that bring any of those into contempt or disrepute; flags, coats of arms, or other governmental insignia; a living individual's name, signature, or portrait used without that individual's written consent; marks that are merely descriptive, deceptively misdescriptive, primarily geographically descriptive or misdescriptive, or primarily merely a surname (each subject to a statutory exception where the mark has become distinctive of the applicant's goods or services through five years of continuous use in California); and, as the statute's own words provide, a mark that "consists of or comprises a mark that so resembles a mark registered in this state or a mark or trade name previously used by another and not abandoned, as to be likely, when used on or in connection with the goods or services of the applicant, to cause confusion or mistake, or to deceive."

citations.cite: grounds for refusing registration of a mark — likelihood of confusion with a previously registered or used mark or trade name
citations.quote: It consists of or comprises a mark that so resembles a mark registered in this state or a mark or trade name previously used by another and not abandoned, as to be likely, when used on or in connection with the goods or services of the applicant, to cause confusion or mistake, or to deceive.

expectedJSON.gap: This clause quotes verbatim only the sixth of Section 14205's six lettered refusal criteria, subdivision (f) (the likelihood-of-confusion ground); the other five are paraphrased, not quoted. More significantly, the first two criteria as written — barring marks that consist of or comprise "immoral, deceptive, or scandalous matter" (subdivision (a)) or matter that may "disparage" persons, institutions, or beliefs (subdivision (b)) — track language nearly identical to federal Lanham Act provisions that the United States Supreme Court held unconstitutional as viewpoint-based restrictions on speech in Matal v. Tam (2017) (the disparagement bar) and Iancu v. Brunetti (2019) (the "immoral or scandalous" bar). This document did not verify either of those decisions, or any California case addressing this state statute's own disparaging/immoral/scandalous language, against a primary source this session: CourtListener's search tool returned a rate-limit error ("429—Rate limit exceeded: 125/day") when queried for this topic, and no case-law citation is included anywhere in this document as a result. This clause should therefore not be read as confirming that Section 14205(a) or (b), as written on the books, is currently enforced by the Secretary of State as written; it reports only the statutory text found at leginfo.legislature.ca.gov, not any judicial narrowing or invalidation of it.

expectedJSON.body: A person who uses a mark may file an application for its registration with the Secretary of State, on a form the Secretary prescribes, setting forth specified information, including the applicant's name and business address, the goods or services and the manner in which the mark is used on or in connection with them, a statement of the applicant's ownership and belief that no other person has a superior right to use the mark, and, as the statute specifically requires, "the date on which the mark was first used anywhere and the date when it was first used in this state by the applicant or a predecessor in interest." The application must include a declaration of accuracy, and the statute attaches a specific consequence to a knowingly false declaration: a person who "willfully states as true in the declaration a material fact that he or she knows to be false" is subject to a civil penalty of up to $10,000, enforceable in an action brought by a public prosecutor, and the statute requires that the declarant be informed of this penalty in writing. The Secretary may also require a statement of any related United States Patent and Trademark Office filing, a drawing of the mark, three specimens showing the mark as actually used, the application fee, and, if the mark is in a language other than English, a certified English translation.

citations.quote: The date on which the mark was first used anywhere and the date when it was first used in this state by the applicant or a predecessor in interest.

citations.cite: civil penalty for a willfully false declaration of accuracy in a state trademark application
citations.quote: If the person signing the declaration willfully states as true in the declaration a material fact that he or she knows to be false, he or she shall be subject to a civil penalty of not more than ten thousand dollars ($10,000).

expectedJSON.gap: This clause quotes two of Section 14207's several requirements — the dual first-use dates in subdivision (a)(3) and the false-declaration penalty in subdivision (d) — and paraphrases the rest; both citations are subdivisions of the same enacted section, not independent statutory sources. This clause does not itself state whether the first-use-anywhere and first-use-in-California dates given in this document would in fact satisfy the statute's dual-date requirement, and does not confirm whether the Secretary of State, as a matter of current administrative practice, still requires every item this 2008-enacted text describes (for example, the specimen and drawing requirements) exactly as written, since this document verified only the statutory text itself, not any current Secretary of State regulation, form instructions, or filing-fee schedule, none of which this document reproduces.

expectedJSON.body: After an application is filed and the fee paid, the Secretary of State may cause the application to be examined for conformity with the Model State Trademark Law, may request additional information or amendments, and, if the applicant is found not entitled to registration, must advise the applicant of the reasons and allow a specified period to reply or amend; this reply-and-reexamine cycle may repeat until the Secretary finally refuses registration or the applicant fails to respond, at which point the application is deemed abandoned. Where the Secretary is concurrently processing more than one application for the same or a confusingly similar mark covering the same or related goods or services, the statute resolves the conflict by filing date: "the secretary shall grant priority to the applications in the order of filing," with any rejected applicant then left to bring a statutory cancellation action against the prior-filed registrant. If the Secretary finally refuses registration, the statute gives the applicant a specific judicial remedy rather than an administrative appeal within the Secretary's own office: "the applicant may seek a writ of mandamus to compel registration," which "may be granted, but without costs to the secretary, on proof that all statements in the application are true and that the mark is otherwise entitled to registration."

citations.quote: In the instance of applications concurrently being processed by the secretary seeking registration of the same or confusingly similar marks for the same or related goods or services, the secretary shall grant priority to the applications in the order of filing.

citations.cite: writ of mandamus as the applicant's remedy for a final refusal of registration
citations.quote: If the secretary finally refuses registration of the mark, the applicant may seek a writ of mandamus to compel registration. A writ may be granted, but without costs to the secretary, on proof that all statements in the application are true and that the mark is otherwise entitled to registration.

The mandamus remedy described here runs against the Secretary of State's refusal to register; this clause does not describe, and this document does not separately address, any private right of action a competing mark owner might have to challenge a registration once issued, which is instead addressed by the cancellation clause below. This clause also does not state the ordinary time limit, if any, within which a mandamus petition must be filed following a final refusal, which this document did not locate in the text of this chapter.

expectedJSON.body: Once an applicant has complied with the chapter's requirements, the statute directs that "the secretary shall cause a certificate of registration to be issued and delivered to the applicant," under the Secretary's signature and the seal of the state, showing the registrant's name and business address, the claimed dates of first use anywhere and first use in California, the class and description of the goods or services, a reproduction of the mark, and the registration date and term. The statute then gives that certificate a specific evidentiary role in state court: "any certificate of registration issued by the secretary under the provisions of this chapter or a copy thereof duly certified by the secretary shall be admissible in evidence as competent and sufficient proof of the registration of the mark in any action or judicial proceeding in any court of this state."

The statutory text quoted here makes the certificate proof of the fact of registration itself; it does not, on its own quoted terms, state that the certificate is prima facie evidence of the mark's validity, of the registrant's ownership, or of an exclusive right to use the mark in commerce — evidentiary presumptions that a different statute, the federal Lanham Act, expressly attaches to a federal registration certificate under 15 U.S.C. expectedJSON.body: A state registration is time-limited and must be affirmatively renewed to continue. The statute provides that "a registration of mark pursuant to this chapter shall be effective for a term of five years from the date of registration and, upon application filed within six months prior to the expiration of the term, in a manner complying with the requirements of the secretary, the registration may be renewed for a like term from the end of the expiring term," accompanied by a renewal fee. The statute further provides that "a registration may be renewed for successive periods of five years in like manner," so that a registration can in principle be kept in force indefinitely through repeated five-year renewals. Every renewal application, whether of a registration made under this chapter or one carried over from a prior state trademark act, must include a verified statement that the mark has been and is still in use, together with a specimen showing that actual use.

citations.quote: A registration of mark pursuant to this chapter shall be effective for a term of five years from the date of registration and, upon application filed within six months prior to the expiration of the term, in a manner complying with the requirements of the secretary, the registration may be renewed for a like term from the end of the expiring term.
A registration may be renewed for successive periods of five years in like manner.

The quoted text states a six-month pre-expiration renewal-filing window; this document did not locate, within this chapter's text, any express grace period or reinstatement procedure for a registration that lapses because no renewal application was filed within that window, and this clause does not state what becomes of an unrenewed registration beyond the fact that Section 14230, addressed in a separate clause below, lists a registration "not renewed in accordance with the provisions of this chapter" as one ground for cancellation.

expectedJSON.body: The statute lists several distinct grounds requiring the Secretary of State to cancel a registration, in whole or in part: a voluntary request from the registrant or record assignee; a court finding that the registered mark has been abandoned, that the registrant is not the mark's owner, that the registration was granted improperly or obtained fraudulently, or that the mark has become the generic name for the goods or services it covers; a court-ordered cancellation on any ground; a dishonored payment check, following notice and a further 30-day cure period; and a registration issued in error within the preceding six months in violation of the confusing-similarity refusal ground. A separate, non-discretionary ground applies simply where a registration was "not renewed in accordance with the provisions of this chapter." The statute also addresses the specific interaction between a state registration and a prior federal one covering the same mark: where a state registration is challenged as confusingly similar to a mark registered earlier with the United States Patent and Trademark Office, "should the registrant prove that the registrant is the owner of a concurrent registration of a mark in the United States Patent and Trademark Office covering an area including this state, the registration hereunder shall not be canceled for that area of the state."

The federal-registration proviso quoted here protects a registrant only for "that area of the state" covered by the registrant's own concurrent federal registration — it does not, on its quoted terms, immunize the state registration statewide, and this clause does not attempt to state how "area" is determined or proven in a cancellation proceeding, which this document did not locate addressed elsewhere in this chapter's text.

expectedJSON.body: The Model State Trademark Law states its own intended relationship to the federal trademark system. The statute recites a legislative intent "to provide a system of state trademark registration and protection substantially consistent with the federal system of trademark registration and protection under the Trademark Act of 1946 (15 U.S.C. Sec. 1051 et seq.), as amended," and directs that federal case law construing the Lanham Act "should be examined as nonbinding authority for interpreting and construing this chapter" — meaning federal decisions inform, but do not control, how a California court or the Secretary of State applies this state statute. A California state registration remains, on this statute's own terms, a separate legal act from any federal registration or application with the United States Patent and Trademark Office; obtaining one does not itself obtain, or substitute for, the other. Separately from this state's relationship to the federal system, this chapter also expressly preserves common-law trademark rights that arise from actual use without any registration at all, a point addressed, with its own citation to this chapter, by this project's existing Trademark Infringement — Cease and Desist Letter Information Sheet document and not repeated here.
